nameStory: The slender arrowhead gets its name from its ultra-narrow, needle-like leaves that look nothing like the classic arrow shape of its cousins. Instead of broad arrowheads, this plant sports leaves so thin they resemble quills from old-fashioned ink pens, earning it the alternate name 'quill-leaved arrowhead.'
description: Slender arrowhead is a graceful aquatic plant that grows up to 2.5 feet tall in shallow water and wetland edges. Unlike other arrowheads with their distinctive arrow-shaped leaves, this species has extremely narrow, grass-like leaves that can grow both underwater and above the surface. In summer, it produces delicate white flowers about half an inch across that rise above the foliage on tall stalks.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Extremely narrow, grass-like leaves that feel smooth and slightly rubbery to the touch, growing both submerged and above water - completely unlike the broad arrow shapes of other arrowheads

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers about half an inch across with three rounded petals, arranged in circular clusters (whorls) on stems that rise well above the leaves

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in shallow water or muddy shores, typically reaching 1-2.5 feet tall with a clumping habit that spreads from underground runners

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, succulent-feeling flower stalks that emerge from the water, often with a slightly triangular cross-section when you roll them between your fingers

habitat: Look for slender arrowhead along the acidic shores of ponds, lakes, and marshes, especially in sphagnum bogs where the water has a tea-like color. It thrives in shallow water and muddy edges of wetlands throughout New England, often growing alongside sedges and other bog plants. This species particularly favors the nutrient-poor, acidic conditions that many other plants can't tolerate.

seasonality.spring: New grass-like shoots emerge from the mud and shallow water, initially all submerged but gradually reaching toward the surface.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with white flowers appearing in July and August on stalks rising above the narrow foliage. This is the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and plants begin to die back, with leaves turning yellow-brown before disappearing beneath the water.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with all above-ground parts gone, surviving as roots and underground runners in the mud.

funFact: This plant is so rare that it's been found in only 48 locations across all of New England, making it one of our most elusive native wildflowers - you're more likely to spot a moose than find a slender arrowhead!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with sedges or grasses growing in water, but slender arrowhead's white three-petaled flowers in summer are the dead giveaway. Remember: if it has narrow leaves in water but blooms with white flowers, you've likely found this rare gem.
contextualKnowledge: Don't expect to see the classic 'arrowhead' leaf shape with this species - it's the oddball of the arrowhead family. Many botanists doing wetland surveys walk right past it assuming it's just another grass or sedge until they notice those telltale white flowers.
compareHints: While broadleaf arrowhead has classic arrow-shaped leaves and grass-leaved arrowhead has broader, ribbon-like foliage, slender arrowhead's leaves are so narrow they look like green needles. The flowers are also smaller than most other arrowheads, and it's the only one that specifically seeks out acidic bog conditions rather than neutral or alkaline waters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Broadleaf arrowhead stands out from its relatives by having the widest, most pronounced arrow-shaped leaves in the genus - while grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, strap-like leaves and slender arrowhead has thin, linear foliage.
Among New England's arrowheads, grass-leaved arrowhead is instantly recognizable by its narrow, grass-like leaves – all other species have distinctly arrow-shaped or oval leaves.
Compared to the common broadleaf arrowhead, Midwestern arrowhead has more narrow, elongated leaf lobes and distinctly shorter beaks on its fruits.
Unlike broadleaf arrowhead with its iconic three-pointed arrow leaves, sessile-fruited arrowhead has narrow ovals.
Among New England's arrowheads, arumleaf arrowhead is distinguished by its relatively broad, triangular leaves that are wider than they are long.
Among the arrowhead family, Engelmann's stands out for its extremely narrow leaf lobes and strict preference for acidic water.
Among New England's arrowheads, Spongy Arrowhead is distinguished by its uniquely soft, air-filled leaf stalks - a feature no other local Sagittaria species shares.
Among New England arrowheads, delta arrowhead has broader, more triangular leaves than the common broadleaf arrowhead, and much wider leaves than the grass-like narrow-leaved arrowhead.
Among New England's arrowheads, this species stands out for having the thinnest, most grass-like leaves - much narrower even than grass-leaved arrowhead.

Among New England arrowheads, hooded arrowhead is unique for its curved sepals that hood over the flower petals, while broadleaf arrowhead has flat, open flowers and grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, grass-like leaves rather than the broad arrow shape.
